description: We are Supernova Syndicate, a team of high school students interested in space, science, technology, and problem-solving. We’re taking on the Planet X and SPHEREx challenge and want to create something useful and creative.
summary:
Almost a century ago, Pluto was discovered with a blink comparator, a machine that flipped between two photos of the sky so that anything that moved would jump out. Today, NASA’s SPHEREx telescope maps the entire sky in 102 infrared colors every six months, but comparing those images by hand is nearly impossible, especially for people without astronomy training.

Our team, Supernova Syndicate, built Sphere Shift, a blink comparator for the SPHEREx era. Type a star name, enter coordinates, or draw a box on an interactive sky map, and the website plays every SPHEREx pass of that spot like a short video. It can subtract one pass from another to reveal what changed, automatically circle anything that brightened, faded, or moved, and show the infrared spectrum of any star you click. Gaia data adds known star positions and motion tracks for comparison.

Sphere Shift turns a massive NASA archive into something anyone can explore in a browser. Students and citizen scientists can watch Barnard’s Star slide across the sky, catch a variable star flickering, and maybe notice something nobody has seen before.
details:
Sphere Shift is a free, public website that lets anyone watch the infrared sky change over time using real NASA SPHEREx data. There are three ways to pick a target: search for an object by name, enter coordinates, or pan around an all-sky map and draw a box anywhere you want to look. The site then gathers every SPHEREx observation of that region, lines the images up, and plays them back like a short video so that moving or flickering objects stand out. Five well-known targets, including Barnard’s Star and the cold brown dwarf WISE 0855, are one click away from the first screen so new users can see a result right away.

Blinking is only the start. Users can switch to a difference view that subtracts one pass from another, or a changes view that compares each difference to the noise in the image and automatically circles anything that stands out by five sigma or more. Each marker has its own shape for brighter, fainter, moved, or variable, and each one opens a card with one-click checks against catalogs like SIMBAD, CatWISE, and Gaia to help answer the question every discoverer asks: is this new? Clicking any star draws its infrared spectrum on the spot. Users can also browse the 102 wavelengths directly, including presets tuned to water ice, carbon dioxide ice, and carbon monoxide. A Gaia DR3 overlay shows known stars with tracks for where they are heading, and a discovery mode searches for moving objects that Gaia does not list. In our testing it found WISE 0855 without being told where to look.

The hardest part was making the comparison honest. A single SPHEREx exposure is not one color, because each detector sits behind a filter whose wavelength changes across the image. If you blink raw exposures, a star can appear to change brightness when it has not changed at all. To solve this, our backend combines all the exposures from one pass and one detector band into a single clean image, matches the wavelengths between passes, and reprojects everything onto the same north-up grid. We also decided the site should always be upfront about its limits. It warns users when a bright star saturates the detector, shades pixels that have no data, and labels whether results are freshly processed or loaded from a saved copy.

We built the frontend with HTML, CSS, and JavaScript, using Aladin Lite for the sky map. The backend is written in Python with FastAPI, and uses Astropy, NumPy, reproject, and photutils to process and measure the images. Our data comes from the SPHEREx archive at NASA’s IRSA, along with Gaia DR3 for star positions and motion. We used GitHub for our code, GitHub Pages to host the site, and Microsoft Azure to run the backend. A weekly automated check looks for new SPHEREx data releases so the tool stays current as the mission continues. AI tools, including Claude, ChatGPT, and Codex, helped us with coding, debugging, and improving the project.

What makes Sphere Shift creative is that it takes a hundred-year-old idea and rebuilds it for a telescope that sees 102 colors. Instead of only showing pictures of space, it gives users the same tools researchers use, explained in plain language. A guided tour, a glossary, and a field guide help beginners understand what they are looking at. Every view has a shareable link, so a teacher can send a class straight to a moving star, and results can be exported as images, movies, or data files. We also considered accessibility by adding keyboard controls, markers that work for color-blind users, a phone layout, and a safety warning before fast flashing.

Our goal is to make real discovery feel possible for students, space enthusiasts, and citizen scientists. NASA collects enormous amounts of information about our universe, and we believe more people should get to explore it. SPHEREx will keep scanning the sky, and every new pass is another chance for someone using Sphere Shift to be the first to notice that something changed.
